extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters deliberating ratification of the U.S. Constitution (readers of the Independent Journal / people of the State of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic political essays arguing and defending the allocation, limits, and practical operation of powers between the proposed federal government and the state governments during Constitutional ratification. Focuses on whether federal powers are necessary, their scope, and safeguards against federal encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of construction/implication for necessary and proper powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the end is required, the means are authorized; wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that positive enumeration of every necessary means would be impossible and dangerous; therefore necessary and proper (implied) powers must be accepted. If Congress misconstrues this part of the Constitution and exercises powers not warranted by its true meaning, remedies lie with the executive and judiciary to expound and give effect to legislative acts, and ultimately with the people by electing different representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against exhaustive positive enumeration of particular powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Had the convention attempted a positive enumeration of the powers necessary and proper for carrying their other powers into effect, the attempt would have involved a complete digest of laws on every subject to which the Constitution relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to enumerate particular means would require accommodation to all possible future changes and would either omit necessary means or turn any omission into a positive grant of authority. Partial enumerations would mislead by selecting the least necessary exceptions and weakening the exception language. Hence, enumeration of particulars is a chimerical and unsafe approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of the federal Constitution, laws, and treaties (Supremacy Clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The supremacy clause is necessary to prevent state constitutions from nullifying federal authority; leaving state constitutions supreme would annul any federal authorities exceeding the Articles of Confederation, create inconsistencies among states about national laws and treaties, and invert the proper relation between the whole and the parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath/affirmation to support the Constitution for state magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is necessary that state magistrates be bound to support the federal Constitution because state officers have essential agency in giving effect to the federal Constitution (e.g., influence on elections). Federal officers need not be similarly bound to state constitutions because federal officers have no role in carrying state constitutions into effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of delegated vs. reserved powers (few and defined vs numerous and indefinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal powers will be exercised principally on external objects (war, peace, negotiation, foreign commerce, taxation connected to commerce). Powers reserved to states extend to ordinary affairs concerning lives, liberties, and properties and the internal order, improvement, and prosperity of the State. Federal operations will be most important in war and danger; state operations in peace and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral and institutional dependence of federal government on the states
rubrics_metrics.description: The President and Senate will depend in many cases on the legislatures of the several States; the Senate will be elected absolutely and exclusively by the State legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because federal officers owe much of their appointment or election to state mechanisms, the federal government will be more likely to feel dependence and to be 'obsequious' rather than overbearing toward the states. This dependence is presented as a structural safeguard against federal encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments' practical advantages against federal encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The State governments will have the advantage whether compared in respect to the immediate dependence of the one on the other; to the weight of personal influence; to the powers respectively vested in them; to the predilection and probable support of the people; to the disposition and faculty of resisting and frustrating the measures of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific advantages listed include: far greater numbers of local officers (justices of the peace, militia officers, county/corporation/town officers), closer acquaintance with the people, greater avenues for patronage and emoluments, and control of many mechanisms (e.g., elections) that shape federal composition and enforcement. These factors make state governments likelier to resist or frustrate federal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as a check on standing federal armies
rubrics_metrics.description: A militia amounting to near half a million of citizens with arms in their hands, officered by men chosen from among themselves... would be able to repel a standing army of twenty-five or thirty thousand men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that even if a large standing army were formed by the federal government, the militia, backed by state governments and popular attachment, forms a practical and potent barrier against federal military usurpation. The argument emphasizes local appointment of militia officers and the people's attachment to state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers principle (concern about mixing of branches)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the principal objections... is its supposed violation of the political maxim, that the legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay introduces this objection as a principal criticism to be examined: whether the particular structure and distribution of powers in the proposed Constitution violate the separation of powers maxim. (Further development of this point is indicated as reserved for subsequent examination.)
